Timeline::shift¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

Timeline Timeline::shift(int periods, std::string_view unit) const

Move Instants By A Runtime-Selected Unit¶

shift() moves every defined instant by the same signed number of temporal units and returns a new Timeline. It exists for code in which the unit is a runtime choice: a parser, command line, configuration file, or user interface can supply unit without requiring a branch at the call site. When the unit is known while writing C++, the named operation such as add_days() or add_hours() states the intent more directly.

The method preserves the receiver’s shape, logical element order, and timezone. NaT remains NaT. It neither mutates the receiver nor shifts positions along an axis; “shift” here means temporal arithmetic on each value.

Parameters And Units¶

Parameter

Meaning

Accepted values

periods

Signed count applied to every defined element

Negative, zero, or positive int

unit

Temporal unit selected at runtime

year, month, day, hour, minute, second, compared without regard to ASCII letter case

There are deliberately no abbreviated or plural aliases. For example, DAY is accepted, but d, days, and day are not. The method does not trim whitespace. Keeping one spelling per concept prevents configuration text from quietly acquiring a second vocabulary.

The units divide into two arithmetic models:

Unit

Arithmetic

Equivalent named method

year

Local-calendar movement with end-of-month clamping

add_years(periods)

month

Local-calendar movement with end-of-month clamping

add_months(periods)

day

Local-calendar movement preserving the displayed clock

add_days(periods)

hour

Fixed elapsed duration

add_hours(periods)

minute

Fixed elapsed duration

add_minutes(periods)

second

Fixed elapsed duration

add_seconds(periods)

Calendar movement is evaluated in tz(). Fixed-duration movement is evaluated on the underlying instant. That difference becomes visible at daylight-saving boundaries.

Example: Dispatch Every Supported Unit¶

const auto leap = pluss::timeline::make("2024-02-29T08:15:30Z");

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(leap.shift(1, "year")) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(leap.shift(1, "month")) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(leap.shift(1, "day")) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(leap.shift(1, "hour")) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(leap.shift(1, "minute")) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(leap.shift(1, "second")) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2025-02-28 08:15:30
Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2024-03-29 08:15:30
Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2024-03-01 08:15:30
Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2024-02-29 09:15:30
Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2024-02-29 08:16:30
Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2024-02-29 08:15:31

The year result demonstrates end-of-month clamping: one calendar year after 29 February 2024 is 28 February 2025. Month movement keeps day 29 because that date exists in March. Day movement crosses the leap-day boundary normally.

Example: Negative, Zero, And Case-Insensitive Dispatch¶

const auto leap = pluss::timeline::make("2024-02-29T08:15:30Z");

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(leap.shift(-1, "DAY")) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(leap.shift(0, "month")) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2024-02-28 08:15:30
Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2024-02-29 08:15:30

A negative count moves backward. Zero still returns a value-equivalent new timeline through the selected operation; it is useful when a signed runtime count naturally includes zero, but should not be used merely to copy an object.

Example: Civil Days Are Not Always Twenty-Four Hours¶

const auto before = pluss::timeline::make("2024-03-09T10:30:00Z")
                        .tz_convert("America/Edmonton");

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(before.shift(1, "day")) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(before.shift(24, "hour")) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=America/Edmonton)
2024-03-10 03:30:00
Timeline(shape=[], tz=America/Edmonton)
2024-03-10 04:30:00

The first operation preserves the local clock while crossing the spring transition, so only 23 elapsed hours pass. The second adds exactly 24 elapsed hours, so its displayed clock is one hour later. Choose day for instructions about the next local calendar day and hour for elapsed-time requirements.

Example: Shape, Timezone, And NaT Are Preserved¶

const auto matrix = pluss::timeline::make({
    {"2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", ""},
    {"2024-01-03T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-04T00:00:00Z"},
}).tz_convert("America/Edmonton");

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(matrix.shift(2, "hour")) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2, 2], tz=America/Edmonton)
[ 2023-12-31 19:00:00                 NaT ]
[ 2024-01-02 19:00:00 2024-01-03 19:00:00 ]

The scalar count broadcasts over all logical positions without changing the two-dimensional geometry. A NaT position is propagated rather than treated as an invalid calendar value.

Example: Noncanonical Text Is Rejected¶

const auto t = pluss::timeline::make("2024-02-29T08:15:30Z");

for (const auto unit : {"years", " day "}) {
  try {
    (void)t.shift(1, unit);
  } catch (const pluss::Error&) {
    std::cout << "rejected\n";
  }
}

Output¶

rejected
rejected

An unsupported unit fails before a result is returned. For a supported unit, calendar-range or duration overflow also throws. Calendar movement is all-or-nothing: the method does not return a partially shifted result if one defined element cannot be represented.

Cost And Allocation¶

shift() is linear in numel() and allocates storage for the result. Calendar units also perform timezone-aware civil conversion per defined element; fixed units use checked integer duration arithmetic. If the unit is constant in a hot path, prefer the corresponding named method to avoid repeated string normalization and dispatch.

See Also¶

  • add_days: direct local-calendar day movement.

  • add_hours: direct elapsed-hour movement.

  • span: measure the relationship between two timelines.
